tagline: A shark disguised as the seafloor
summary: Flattened, blotched and fringed with branching skin flaps around its mouth, the spotted wobbegong looks more like a patterned rug than a shark. It rests on Australian reefs by day and hunts fishes, octopuses and crabs at night.

stats.depth: Usually 0–110 m; recorded to about 220 m
stats.range: Southern Australia, from Western Australia to southern Queensland

facts.title: A fringed disguise
facts.text: Along each side of the head, in front of the eye, are 6–10 long, branching skin flaps called dermal lobes. With its blotched, ringed pattern they help this well-camouflaged shark blend into reef and sand.

facts.title: Night shift
facts.text: Spotted wobbegongs are nocturnal: they usually rest during the day and feed at night, mostly on fishes and octopuses, plus crabs and crayfish.

facts.title: Big litters
facts.text: Females give birth to live young — up to 37 pups — after a gestation of 10–11 months. Inside the mother, the embryos feed only on their egg yolk.

facts.title: A shark out of water
facts.text: It can be found in water barely deep enough to cover it, and has been seen climbing between tide pools with its back out of the water.

facts.title: Docile — until stepped on
facts.text: Though usually placid, it bites people who step on or provoke it, can cause severe cuts, and is often reluctant to let go.

image.alt: A spotted wobbegong lying across a reef covered in orange and cream sponges, its flat greenish-brown body patterned with pale rings, and a fringe of small branching flaps along its mouth
image.caption: A spotted wobbegong resting among sponges off Forster, New South Wales
image.creator: Taso Viglas

gallery.alt: Head-on view of a spotted wobbegong lying on shelly sand, its broad flat head fringed with branching flaps and its back patterned with pale rings
gallery.caption: Head-on, the wobbegong's 'beard' of dermal lobes is easy to see
gallery.creator: Christopher Mark

notes: Size: Fishes of Australia gives max 170 cm; FishBase cites an older max of 320 cm — used the more conservative figure. IUCN: Least Concern (assessed 2015) per FishBase; Fishes of Australia page inconsistently shows both Near Threatened and Least Concern, and notes it is listed as Vulnerable in New South Wales. Rejected Commons 'Orectolobus maculatus kurnell.jpg' — its banded pattern looks more like O. halei/ornatus. Tide-pool climbing is an older field observation (FishBase citing Compagno), hence 'uncertain'.
